new.title: See Paula Modersohn-Becker's art in Böttcherstraße
new.desc: The Paula Modersohn-Becker Museum opened in 1927 as the first museum in the world devoted to a woman painter. The coffee merchant Ludwig Roselius commissioned the Expressionist brick building from Bernhard Hoetger, and it shows major works from every phase of her short life.
new.tip: Look at the building before you go in: Hoetger shaped the brick facade like a sculpture. One ticket also covers the neighbouring Roselius house.

new.title: Face the concrete of the Bunker Valentin
new.desc: On the Weser at Farge stands the largest free-standing bunker in Germany, built from 1943 to 1945 as a submarine factory that never went into production. Between 10,000 and 12,000 forced labourers were made to build it, and thousands of them died. Since 2015 it has been a memorial with a visitor centre.
new.tip: It lies far out in the north of Bremen, so allow half a day. A marked route with information points leads around and into the building.
new.q: Denkort Bunker Valentin, Rekumer Siel, Bremen

new.title: See contemporary art in the Weserburg warehouses
new.desc: The Weserburg fills four former warehouses on the Teerhof, the narrow peninsula between the Weser and the Kleine Weser. When it opened in 1991 it was the first collectors' museum in Europe, showing works lent by private collectors across 6,000 square metres.
new.tip: The upper floors give good views of the river on both sides. The Teerhof footbridge links the museum with the Schlachte.
new.q: Weserburg Museum für moderne Kunst, Teerhof 20, Bremen

new.title: Swim with the students at the Unisee
new.desc: The Stadtwaldsee, which everyone calls the Unisee because the university is next door, is a former gravel pit of 28 hectares and up to 16.5 metres deep. On the side facing the campus there are lawns and a sandy beach, and on the north-east shore a nudist beach.
new.tip: In hot summers the lake is sometimes closed to swimmers because of algae, so check before you pack your towel. It is an easy bike ride through the Bürgerpark and Stadtwald.

new.title: Spend a summer evening at the Breminale
new.desc: For five days each summer the meadows of the Osterdeich turn into a free open-air festival along the Weser. Several stages host live music, joined by film, readings, performance and a family programme, and around 200,000 people come.
new.tip: Entry is free, so drift from stage to stage. Come by bike or tram, as the streets of the Viertel behind the dyke fill up fast.

new.title: Walk the high bank of the Lesum in Knoops Park
new.desc: Knoops Park in St. Magnus covers 65 hectares on the steep north bank of the Lesum. The merchant Ludwig Knoop had it laid out from 1870 by Wilhelm Benque, the designer of the Bürgerpark. His mansion, Schloss Mühlenthal, was pulled down in 1933, but the old trees and viewpoints over the river remain.
new.tip: Take the train to Bremen-St. Magnus and walk down to the river from there. The path along the top of the slope has the best views.

new.title: Eat your way around Markthalle Acht
new.desc: In the market hall on the Domshof, small stalls cook dishes from around the world: Hawaiian bowls, burritos, Korean and Pakistani food, Spanish and Italian plates, and plenty of cake. The stallholders work to a shared motto of less but better, with regional and seasonal produce.
new.tip: The hall also hosts live music, a repair café and flea markets, so look at the programme. Opening days vary, so check before you go on a Sunday or Monday.

new.title: Drink unfiltered beer at the Union Brauerei
new.desc: The Union brewery in Walle was founded in 1907 by local innkeepers and closed in 1968. Since 2015 beer has been brewed again on the same spot, in a new brewhouse set inside the old brick building. The beers are neither filtered nor heat-treated, and the brewpub has a covered beer garden.
new.tip: Brewery tours with a tasting can be booked in advance. The brewpub is usually closed on Sundays and Mondays.

new.title: Shop for lunch at the Findorffmarkt
new.desc: The weekly market on the square off Neukirchstraße is one of the biggest in Bremen and the heart of the Findorff neighbourhood. Farmers, bakers, cheese sellers and fishmongers set up on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday mornings.
new.tip: Saturday is the liveliest day, when half the neighbourhood meets here for coffee. Stalls start to pack up around one o'clock.

new.title: Sip fresh roast in the old Kaffee HAG works
new.desc: Lloyd Caffee, Bremen's oldest traditional roastery, works in the former Kaffee HAG factory at the Holzhafen. Ludwig Roselius, who brought decaffeinated coffee to market in 1906, built a marble hall here in 1914 with white Carrara marble and Art Nouveau display cases. Today the roastery has a shop and café.
new.tip: The marble hall is shown on the roastery's tours and coffee seminars, which need to be booked. Without a booking you can still drink a cup and buy beans.

new.title: Order Knipp and fried potatoes at the Kaiser Friedrich
new.desc: The Gasthof zum Kaiser Friedrich has been an inn since 1889, which makes it the oldest in Bremen, in a listed house from around 1630. The rooms have barely changed, and the kitchen cooks North German classics such as Knipp, with a lunch menu that changes. Regulars' tables still meet here, including one of former senators.
new.tip: The fried potatoes are the house pride. Book ahead in the evening, as the rooms are small.
new.q: Gasthof zum Kaiser Friedrich, Lange Wieren 13, Bremen

new.title: Eat at the last pub before New York
new.desc: Deep inside Bremerhaven's overseas port, on the old banana pier, the Treffpunkt Kaiserhafen calls itself the last pub before New York. Sailors, dockers and day trippers share the tables over fish and meat dishes, with car carriers that hold thousands of vehicles moored right outside.
new.tip: It takes cash only. The kitchen serves at lunchtime and again in the evening, with a break in the afternoon.

new.title: Board the Schulschiff Deutschland
new.desc: Germany's last full-rigged ship was launched in 1927 at the Tecklenborg yard in what is now Bremerhaven, as a training ship for merchant sailors. The three-master is 86 metres long and carried 25 sails. After many years moored in Bremen-Vegesack it now lies all year in Bremerhaven's Neuer Hafen.
new.tip: Check the visiting hours first, as the ship is also used for events. From the quay you get the best photo of the full rig.

new.title: Wander among the statues of Thieles Garten
new.desc: The brothers Gustav and Georg Thiele bought this plot in the north of Bremerhaven in 1923 and turned it into a private sculpture garden. Between ponds and exotic trees stand figures made of concrete and wire, many modelled on Georg's wife, the painter Grete Thiele, along with a moor cottage and a house in Moorish style. The city bought the garden in 1985.
new.tip: It is in the Leherheide district, well away from the harbour sights. Check the opening days before you set out.

new.title: Brave the storm at Windstärke 10 in Cuxhaven
new.desc: This museum in two former fish-processing halls by Cuxhaven's fishing harbour tells of shipwrecks and of a hundred years of deep-sea fishing. It was formed in 2013 from the town's old wreck museum and its fishery museum, and covers about 4,000 square metres.
new.tip: It pairs well with a fish lunch in the harbour next door. The room of the Cuxhaven pilots shows how ships are still guided up the Elbe today.

new.title: Visit the brick collegiate church of Bassum
new.desc: The church of St. Mauritius and St. Viktor was built in the 13th century for the women's foundation of Bassum. The brick building mixes late Romanesque and early Gothic forms, with a square tower over the crossing and a hall nave. Inside is a wooden memorial to the abbess Eleonora von Estorff, who died in 1769.
new.tip: The half-timbered buildings of the foundation stand right beside the church. Bassum is on the railway line between Bremen and Osnabrück.

new.title: Ride the Moorexpress through the Teufelsmoor
new.desc: At weekends and on public holidays from May to early October, historic diesel railcars run between Bremen and Stade on a line opened between 1909 and 1911 to reach the peat villages. The Moorexpress stops in Worpswede, Gnarrenburg and Bremervörde, and the ride from Bremen to Bremervörde takes about two hours.
new.tip: Bikes are welcome on board, so you can ride one way and cycle back. Buy tickets ahead on sunny weekends.

new.title: Take a steam train from Bruchhausen-Vilsen
new.desc: The narrow-gauge line from Bruchhausen-Vilsen to Asendorf has carried museum trains since 1966, which makes it the first museum railway in Germany. Volunteers run it as a living open-air museum, mostly with steam engines, over almost eight kilometres of track.
new.tip: Trains run at weekends from May to September and again in December. Look into the workshop, where old skills such as riveting boilers are kept alive.

new.title: Watch the wolf packs at the Wolfcenter Dörverden
new.desc: The Wolfcenter in Dörverden, south of Verden, keeps wolves in large enclosures and explains how they live and how people and wolves can get along. A big multimedia exhibition covers the return of wild wolves to Germany.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, and hours are shorter in winter. Special evenings include howling at the full moon.
